name: Semantic Layers
title: Semantic Layers
answer: A semantic layer defines business terms, metrics and relationships on top of raw tables, so that revenue or active customer means one agreed thing. Text to SQL systems that use one produce far more consistent answers than systems reading raw column names. It sits between the warehouse and the people or models asking questions, and it is the difference between a query tool that guesses at schema and one that speaks the organisation's own vocabulary.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A semantic layer is usually a metadata service rather than a store of data. It holds definitions, joins, hierarchies and metric formulas, and it compiles those into SQL that runs against the underlying warehouse, most often PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery or Databricks. Model context protocol servers are one common way to expose those definitions to an assistant, and this site currently tracks 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses out of 2526 active servers.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with modelling: naming entities, agreeing grain, writing metric definitions once and mapping them to physical columns. Those definitions are then served through an API or a query interface, and a text to SQL system retrieves the relevant terms before generating SQL rather than reading raw column names. Practitioners spend most of their time on curation and testing, checking that a question about active customers resolves to the same calculation every time, and on keeping the model in step with schema changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because a semantic layer concentrates meaning in one place, it also concentrates responsibility. Ownership of each metric needs to be clear, changes need review, and access rules should follow the definitions rather than being reimplemented in every downstream tool. Provenance matters too: a generated answer should be traceable to the metric version and the tables it drew on, so that an audit can reconstruct how a number was produced.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward semantic layers that assistants can read directly, so that definitions travel with the question instead of being rediscovered each time. Expect more standard ways to publish metrics and relationships to agents, and more emphasis on versioning and lineage as generated SQL becomes routine. The open question is not whether models can write SQL but whether the organisation can keep one agreed meaning for the words it asks about.
